pos: v. (to turn from sin to God; to change the mind so that the life turns with it)
etymology: Latin re-, again, and poenitere, to cause regret — which is why the English word leans toward sorrow. The Greek metanoeo means to change the mind, and the Hebrew shub simply means to turn round. Between the three lies most of the confusion about this word.
biblical_def: To repent is to turn. Peter joins the two verbs: “Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Act 3:19). It is commanded universally: God “now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Act 17:30). It is distinguished from mere misery: “godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death” (2Co 7:10). It is tested by what follows: “Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance” (Mat 3:8). And the prodigal shows its shape in one sentence — a change of mind that becomes a change of direction: “I will arise and go to my father” (Luk 15:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines repentance as sorrow for any thing done or said; and, in theology, the pain, regret or affliction which a person feels on account of his past conduct, because it exposes him to punishment — distinguishing this legal repentance from evangelical repentance, which is accompanied with hatred of sin and a determination to forsake it.
webster_full: REPENT, v.i. To feel pain, sorrow or regret for something done or spoken.
2. To express sorrow for something past.
3. In theology, to sorrow or be pained for sin, as a violation of God's holy law, and to determine on a reformation of life; to be penitent.
REPENTANCE, n. Real penitence; sorrow or deep contrition for sin, as an offense and dishonor to God, a violation of his holy law, and the basest ingratitude toward a Being of infinite benevolence.
Repentance is a change of mind, or a conversion from sin to God.
scriptures: Act 3:19
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Mat 3:8
Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:
I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,
corruption_summary: Repentance is reduced to feeling sorry, and Webster's own entry distinguishes the sorrow that fears punishment from the sorrow that hates the sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Corinthians 7:10 divides the whole subject with one sentence, and the two sorrows look identical from outside. Godly sorrow worketh repentance — it produces something, it moves — and the repentance it produces is never regretted afterwards. The sorrow of the world worketh death, and it can be intense, tearful and prolonged. Judas had it. What distinguishes them is not depth of feeling but direction: one runs toward God and one runs away, and a man weeping over consequences may be doing either.

The English word is part of the problem, since repent carries penitence in its Latin bones while the Greek metanoeo means simply to change the mind and the Hebrew shub means to turn round. Both biblical words are about reorientation, and neither specifies an emotion. That is a mercy for temperaments that do not weep easily and a warning to those that do, because tears are not the article and a man may produce them on demand without turning an inch.

The test Scripture gives is fruit, and John the Baptist gave it to a crowd that had come out to be baptised: bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance — fruits answerable to it, proportionate. When they asked what that meant he gave three trades three specific answers: share your coat, exact no more than is appointed, do violence to no man and be content with your wages. Not one of them is about feeling. Repentance in Scripture is verified in the ordinary conduct of the following week, which is why the prodigal's turning point is a sentence about walking: I will arise and go to my father.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn, return; nacham (H5162), to be sorry, comforted; Greek metanoeo (G3340), to change the mind; epistrepho (G1994), to turn about, be converted.
roots_lines: Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, return; Ezekiel 18:30–32, Hosea 6:1, Joel 2:12–13, Isaiah 55:7.
Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind; Matthew 4:17, Acts 2:38, 17:30, Revelation 2:5.
Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, be converted; Acts 3:19, 26:18, 1 Thessalonians 1:9.
usage: “Repent ye therefore, and be converted” — two verbs, one turning.
“Godly sorrow worketh repentance… not to be repented of” — it produces, and is never regretted.
“Fruits meet for repentance” — answerable to it, and none of them a feeling.

pos: n. and v. (censure or disgrace cast upon a man; and, in Scripture, the shame a believer bears for Christ's sake)
etymology: Old French reprochier, from Latin prope, near — to bring a thing back near to a man, to hold it up before his face. A reproach is a charge kept close enough that he cannot look away from it.
biblical_def: Reproach is disgrace laid on a man, and Scripture treats it as a currency Christ's people deliberately accept. Moses chose it: “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward” (Heb 11:26). The church is summoned to it: “let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13). Peter turns it into evidence: “If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you” (1Pe 4:14). It fell first on Christ: “the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me” (Psa 69:9). And a different reproach is to be avoided: an elder “must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (1Ti 3:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reproach as censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious or opprobrious language; and shame, infamy, disgrace.
webster_full: REPROACH, v.t. To censure in terms of opprobrium or contempt.
2. To upbraid; to suggest blame for any thing.
3. To treat with scorn or contempt.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious or opprobrious language towards any person; abusive reflections.
2. Shame; infamy; disgrace.
3. Object of contempt, scorn or derision.
scriptures: Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.
Psa 69:9
For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me.
Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.
corruption_summary: Every reproach a Christian attracts is claimed as the reproach of Christ, and Scripture keeps two kinds carefully apart.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 11:26 makes reproach a thing a man can esteem — weigh, price, count — and Moses is said to have valued it above the treasures of Egypt, which he had actually seen. The verse is an act of accounting, not of stoicism. He had respect unto the recompence of the reward, meaning he looked at what was on the other side, and the reproach came out light. That is the only way reproach is ever borne well: not by pretending it does not hurt but by having something on the scale against it.

First Peter 4:14 promises the spirit of glory to the reproached, and the very next verse closes the loophole: let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. The last item is the one that catches Christians. A man may attract genuine contempt by rudeness, by meddling, by an ungracious manner that has nothing of Christ in it, and then file the result under persecution. Peter names that exact case and excludes it from the blessing.

First Timothy 3:7 shows the other direction and is routinely ignored by people who quote the first. An overseer must have a good report of them which are without — a decent reputation among unbelievers — lest he fall into reproach. So the church is not indifferent to what outsiders think; it cares about it enough to make it a qualification for office. The distinction is between the reproach that attaches to Christ's name and the reproach a man earns for himself, and the difference is usually obvious to everyone except him.
roots_summary: Hebrew cherpah (H2781), reproach, disgrace; charaph (H2778), to reproach, taunt; Greek oneidismos (G3680), reproach; oneidizo (G3679), to revile, upbraid.
roots_lines: Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, shame; Psalm 69:7–9, 69:19–20, Joshua 5:9, Nehemiah 1:3.
Greek oneidismos (G3680) — reproach; Hebrews 11:26, 13:13, 10:33, Romans 15:3.
Greek oneidizo (G3679) — to reproach, revile; 1 Peter 4:14, Matthew 5:11, Mark 15:32.
usage: “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches” — an act of accounting.
“Bearing his reproach” — and it is without the camp.
“A good report of them which are without” — the other half, made a qualification.

pos: n. phrase (the ceasing from self-justifying labour into which a believer enters by trusting Christ's finished work)
etymology: Rest from Old English ræst, repose; the theological phrase is drawn from Hebrews 4, where the Greek katapausis (a settling down, a ceasing) and sabbatismos (a sabbath-keeping) are used of what remains for the people of God.
biblical_def: The rest of faith is entered by believing rather than by achieving. Hebrews states the ground: “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his” (Heb 4:9–10). Entry is by faith: “we which have believed do enter into rest” (Heb 4:3). And yet it is pursued with effort: “Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief” (Heb 4:11). The Lord offers it in two stages: “Come unto me… and I will give you rest… and ye shall find rest unto your souls” (Mat 11:28–29). And its oldest form is a Presence: “My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest” (Exo 33:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rest as cessation of motion or action of any kind, and applicable to any body or being; quiet; repose; and, in Scripture, the final enjoyment of God in heaven.
webster_full: REST, n. Cessation of motion or action of any kind, and applicable to any body or being; as rest from labor.
2. Quiet; repose; a state free from motion or disturbance; a state of reconciliation to God.
3. Sleep; as, retire to rest.
4. Final sleep; death.
5. Place of repose; and, in Scripture, the future enjoyment of God in heaven, or eternal blessedness.
scriptures: Heb 4:9
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
Heb 4:3
For we which have believed do enter into rest, as he said, As I have sworn in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest: although the works were finished from the foundation of the world.
Heb 4:11
Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.
corruption_summary: Rest is preached as passivity, and Hebrews commands labour to enter it in the verse immediately after describing it.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 4:10 and 4:11 stand next to each other and appear to contradict. He that is entered into his rest hath ceased from his own works; and then, let us labour therefore to enter into that rest. Both are meant. The works ceased from are the works by which a man would establish his own standing, and they are abandoned entirely; the labour commanded is the labour of believing, of not drifting, of not repeating Israel's example of unbelief. Every generation of Christians has collapsed one clause into the other — into striving that never rests, or into a rest that never labours.

Matthew 11:28–29 has the same double shape and it is easy to read past. I will give you rest — a gift, received by coming. Then: take my yoke upon you, and learn of me… and ye shall find rest unto your souls — a rest found, by wearing a yoke. The first is justification and is instantaneous; the second is the settled quiet of a soul under Christ's government, and it is learned over years. A believer who has the first and not the second is genuinely saved and genuinely exhausted, and the remedy is not more effort but a different master.

Exodus 33:14 gives the oldest and simplest statement, and it identifies rest with a Person rather than a condition: My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest. Moses had just been offered the land without the Presence and refused it — if thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence. That is the whole doctrine in a negotiation. Rest is not the absence of trouble, since Moses had forty years of it ahead; it is the presence of God in the middle of it.
roots_summary: Greek katapausis (G2663), a settling down, rest; sabbatismos (G4520), a sabbath-keeping; anapauo (G373), to give rest; Hebrew nuach (H5117), to rest, settle.
roots_lines: Greek katapausis (G2663) — rest, a settling down; Hebrews 3:11, 3:18, 4:1–11, Acts 7:49.
Greek sabbatismos (G4520) — a sabbath rest, a keeping of sabbath; Hebrews 4:9 only.
Greek anapauo / anapausis (G373, G372) — to give rest / rest; Matthew 11:28–29, Revelation 14:13.
usage: “He also hath ceased from his own works” — those works, and not all work.
“Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest” — the next verse.
“My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest” — a Person, not a condition.

pos: v. (to bring back to a former and better state; to make good what was lost, broken or taken)
etymology: Latin restaurare, to rebuild, renew. The Hebrew shub behind most Old Testament uses is the same verb rendered repent — a turning back — which is why restoration and repentance are so often the same movement seen from two sides.
biblical_def: To restore is to bring back what was lost. God does it to a soul: “He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake” (Psa 23:3). David asks for it after a great fall, and notice what he asks for: “Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation” (Psa 51:12) — the joy, not the salvation. God promises it to a ruined nation: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten” (Joe 2:25). The church is commanded to do it to a fallen brother: “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). And it is the shape of the end: “the times of restitution of all things” (Act 3:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines restore as to return to a former place or state; to bring back; to repair; to recover from injury; to heal; and to bring back or recover from lapse, degeneracy, doubts or errors.
webster_full: RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former place or state; to bring or send back.
2. To repair; to rebuild.
3. To heal; to cure; to recover from disease; as, to restore health.
4. To make restitution or satisfaction for a thing taken.
5. To recover from lapse, degeneracy, declension or ruin; as, to restore one to the favor of God.
scriptures: Psa 23:3
He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.
Joe 2:25
And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Act 3:21
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
corruption_summary: Restoration is treated as forgiveness alone, and Scripture attaches to it a specific manner, a specific warning, and often a bill.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 6:1 is the most practical verse in the New Testament on restoring a fallen brother, and every clause is load-bearing. It is addressed to ye which are spiritual, which disqualifies the eager. The verb is the one used for setting a broken bone and for mending nets — slow, skilled work, not a pronouncement. It specifies the manner: in the spirit of meekness. And it ends with the clause the restorer needs most: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. A man who approaches a fallen brother without that sentence running in his head will do damage, however correct his doctrine.

Psalm 51:12 is exact about what sin costs a believer and what it does not. David does not ask to be restored to salvation; he asks for the restoration of its joy, and for a right spirit to be renewed within him. That distinction has kept many a Christian from despair after a serious fall and has kept many another from presumption, since the loss is real and severe even where the standing is secure. What sin takes from a believer is the enjoyment of what he still has.

Joel 2:25 is the promise people cling to and it should be quoted whole, because the years are restored by the God who names the locusts as my great army which I sent among you. The devastation was judgment, not accident. That is what makes the promise worth anything: the One restoring is the One who took it away, and He does not restore by pretending the ruin did not happen. Acts 3:21 puts the same logic at the end of history — the times of restitution of all things — which is not a return to Eden but something further on, a creation delivered from the bondage of corruption.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn, restore; shalam (H7999), to make whole, repay; Greek katartizo (G2675), to mend, set in order; apokatastasis (G605), restitution.
roots_lines: Hebrew shub (H7725) — to bring back, restore; Psalm 23:3, 51:12, Joel 2:25, Isaiah 1:26.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, restore, set a bone; Galatians 6:1, Matthew 4:21, 1 Thessalonians 3:10, Hebrews 13:21.
Greek apokatastasis (G605) — restitution, restoration; Acts 3:21 only.
usage: “He restoreth my soul” — and then leadeth, in the same verse.
“Considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” — the clause the restorer needs.
“The years that the locust hath eaten” — and He had sent them.

pos: n. phrase (the glorified body the redeemed receive at Christ's coming — the same body raised, transformed and made immortal)
etymology: Latin resurgere, to rise again. The doctrine is the church's answer to the Greek hope of a soul escaping the body: Christianity's hope is a body raised, and the creed says so in as many words.
biblical_def: The resurrection body is the believer's own body, raised and glorified. Paul sets out four contrasts: “It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: it is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: it is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1Co 15:42–44). The change is necessary: “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1Co 15:53). The pattern is Christ's: He “shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body” (Php 3:21). The likeness is promised: “we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1Jn 3:2). And His own risen body was handled: “a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have” (Luk 24:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines resurrection as a rising again, particularly the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave, particularly at the general judgment.
webster_full: RESURRECTION, n. A rising again; the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave, particularly at the general judgment.
By the resurrection of Christ we have assurance of the future resurrection of men. 1 Cor. 15.
IMMORTALITY, n. The quality of never ceasing to live or exist; exemption from death and annihilation; life destined to endure without end.
scriptures: So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
Php 3:21
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
corruption_summary: “Spiritual body” is read as a body made of spirit, and Paul uses the same adjective in the same letter of ordinary Christians.
corruption_paragraphs: The decisive misreading is of one adjective. Paul contrasts a natural body (psuchikos, soulish) with a spiritual body (pneumatikos), and neither word names a material. He uses the same pair in chapter two for the natural man and the spiritual man, where nobody imagines the spiritual man is made of vapour. The adjective describes what animates and governs a thing. The resurrection body is a real body wholly under the Spirit's rule — incorruptible, glorious, powerful — and the whole force of the chapter is that it is this body, sown and raised, rather than a replacement issued at the graveside.

That is why Luke 24:39 is doctrine and not merely narrative. The disciples supposed they had seen a spirit, and the Lord answered with the most physical demonstration available: handle me and see, for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have — and then He ate a piece of broiled fish in front of them. He showed them the wounds. Whatever glorification did to that body, it did not remove it, and He has not laid it down since; there is a Man in heaven.

The practical consequence reaches into how Christians grieve and how they live. A funeral consoled entirely by the soul's release has borrowed from Plato, and 1 Corinthians 15 offers something better and stranger: the body in the ground is a seed, and what is sown is what comes up. It also settles ethics. If the body is destined for glory, then what is done in it matters permanently, chronic illness is not the last word on a life, and the care of a dying person's body is not a low task. First John 3:2 supplies the one detail that outranks all the others: it doth not yet appear what we shall be, but we shall be like him.
roots_summary: Greek anastasis (G386), resurrection; psuchikos / pneumatikos (G5591, G4152), natural / spiritual; aphtharsia (G861), incorruption; metaschematizo (G3345), to change the fashion of.
roots_lines: Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection, a standing up again; 1 Corinthians 15:42, John 11:25, Acts 17:32, Philippians 3:10.
Greek psuchikos / pneumatikos (G5591, G4152) — natural / spiritual; 1 Corinthians 15:44–46, and of men, 2:14–15.
Greek metaschematisei (G3345) — shall change the fashion of; Philippians 3:21.
usage: “Sown in corruption… raised in incorruption” — the same thing, sown and raised.
“A spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have” — and then He ate.
“We shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is”.

pos: n. phrase (the personal, visible and bodily coming again of Jesus Christ in glory)
etymology: The New Testament's words are parousia (a presence, an arrival), epiphaneia (an appearing) and apokalupsis (an unveiling) — three angles on one event, and each governs a different aspect of how the church is told to wait.
biblical_def: The return of Christ is personal and bodily. The angels state it at the ascension: “this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven” (Act 1:11). It is audible and public: “the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God” (1Th 4:16). Its date is withheld: “But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only” (Mat 24:36). It is the church's posture: “Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13). And the Bible's last words but one are His: “Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines advent as, in the church, a coming; the coming of our Savior; and applies the word to the four weeks before Christmas, and to the second coming, or advent to judgment.
webster_full: ADVENT, n. A coming; appropriately the coming of our Savior, and in the calendar, it includes four sabbaths before Christmas.
COMING, n. The act of coming; approach.
2. The state of being come; arrival.
The second coming of Christ, is his coming to judgment.
scriptures: Act 1:11
Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
corruption_summary: The return is turned into a chart or into an embarrassment, and Scripture makes it the ordinary motive of ordinary obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 24:36 is the plainest sentence in the Bible about prophetic chronology and it has been overridden in every century since it was spoken: of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only. Every date that has been set was set against that verse by someone confident he had found the exception. The Lord's own application of His ignorance-clause is not curiosity but readiness — watch therefore, be ye also ready, for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh — and the parables that follow are about a servant working while the master is away.

The opposite error is quieter and commoner in respectable churches: the return is affirmed in the creed and functions in nobody's week. But the New Testament uses it constantly as leverage on present conduct, and rarely as a subject in its own right. Titus 2 makes the blessed hope the reason to live soberly, righteously and godly in this present world. First John says every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself. First Corinthians 15 ends its resurrection chapter with therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord. The doctrine's purpose is Monday.

Acts 1:11 fixes the manner and forecloses the spiritualising readings. This same Jesus — the one they had eaten with — shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go. Bodily, visibly, personally. The two men in white apparel say it to men standing there gazing up, and the rebuke in the question is gentle: why stand ye gazing up into heaven? They were then sent to a room to pray and shortly afterwards to the ends of the earth. That is the whole shape of Christian waiting — a certainty about the ending, and work in the meantime.
roots_summary: Greek parousia (G3952), a presence, coming; epiphaneia (G2015), an appearing; apokalupsis (G602), an unveiling; gregoreo (G1127), to watch.
roots_lines: Greek parousia (G3952) — coming, arrival, presence; Matthew 24:3, 1 Thessalonians 4:15, 2 Peter 3:4, James 5:7–8.
Greek epiphaneia (G2015) — appearing, manifestation; Titus 2:13, 2 Timothy 4:1, 4:8, 2 Thessalonians 2:8.
Greek apokalupsis (G602) — revelation, unveiling; 1 Corinthians 1:7, 2 Thessalonians 1:7, 1 Peter 1:7, 1:13.
usage: “This same Jesus… shall so come in like manner” — bodily, and visibly.
“But my Father only” — and every date has been set against it.
“Even so, come, Lord Jesus” — the Bible's last prayer.

pos: n. phrase (the recompense Christ promises His people at His coming, distinguished from the salvation which is wholly of grace)
etymology: Old French rewarder, to regard, look upon — a reward is what is given upon a regarding. The Greek misthos is a workman's wage, and the New Testament uses it deliberately of what grace gives to those who had earned nothing.
biblical_def: A reward in heaven is promised to the persecuted: “Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you” (Mat 5:12). It is where treasure is to be sent: “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20). It is assessed by fire, and the man is distinguished from the work: “If any man's work abide… he shall receive a reward. If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire” (1Co 3:14–15). All appear for it: “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2Co 5:10). And Christ brings it Himself: “behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be” (Rev 22:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reward as recompense, or equivalent return for good done, for kindness, for services and the like; and the fruit of men's labor or works.
webster_full: REWARD, n. Recompense, or equivalent return for good done, for kindness, for services and the like.
The laborer is worthy of his reward. 1 Tim. 5.
2. The fruit of men's labor or works.
The dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward. Eccles. 9.
3. A bribe; a gift to pervert judgment.
scriptures: Mat 5:12
Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward.
If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.
And, behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be.
corruption_summary: Reward is either dismissed as mercenary or confused with salvation, and Scripture keeps it as a real motive and a separate account.
corruption_paragraphs: The first instinct of a Christian trained on grace is to be embarrassed by reward, as though working for one were beneath a son. Scripture is not embarrassed. The Lord promises it constantly and by name; Moses had respect unto the recompence of the reward; Hebrews says God is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him, and puts that clause inside the definition of the faith without which it is impossible to please Him. What Scripture forbids is not working for reward but working for the wrong one — the applause of men, received in full on the spot, with nothing owing from heaven.

The second confusion is more serious. First Corinthians 3:15 draws a line that must not be blurred: if any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss, but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. The work is assessed; the man is not on trial. Salvation is by grace through faith, not of works; reward is according to work, and the two run on separate accounts and are settled at the same session. A believer whose life's labour proves to be wood, hay and stubble loses something real and does not lose Christ — and the picture of a man escaping through flames with nothing in his hands is not offered as a comfort.

Matthew 6 gives the mechanism for sending treasure ahead, and it is not a metaphor for feeling generous. The alms, the prayer and the fast done to be seen have their reward already, receipted in full; the same three done in secret are seen by the Father who shall reward openly. That is a transfer, and it is the only investment available with those guarantees: where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal. The verse that follows is the reason it matters — for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. A man's affections migrate to wherever his holdings are, so the location of the holdings is a pastoral question.
roots_summary: Greek misthos (G3408), wages, reward; thesauros (G2344), treasure; apecho (G568), to have in full; zemioo (G2210), to suffer loss.
roots_lines: Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, reward; Matthew 5:12, 6:1–16, 1 Corinthians 3:8–14, Revelation 22:12.
Greek zemiothesetai (G2210) — he shall suffer loss; 1 Corinthians 3:15, Philippians 3:8, Matthew 16:26.
Greek misthapodotes (G3406) — a rewarder; Hebrews 11:6 only.
usage: “Great is your reward in heaven” — promised, by name, to the persecuted.
“He himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire” — the work burns, the man does not.
“Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” — affections follow holdings.

pos: n. phrase (anger aroused by what is genuinely evil, held without sin)
etymology: Righteous from Old English rihtwis, right-wise; anger from Old Norse angr, grief or affliction — the Norse root carries sorrow in it, which is exactly what distinguishes the righteous kind from the other.
biblical_def: Righteous anger is anger at evil, held without sin. It is permitted and bounded in one verse: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath” (Eph 4:26). The Lord shows it, and its companion emotion is named: He “looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts” (Mar 3:5). He acts on it in the temple, having made “a scourge of small cords” (John 2:15). It is an attribute of God: “God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day” (Psa 7:11). And the standing caution stands beside all of it: “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jas 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines anger as a violent passion of the mind excited by a real or supposed injury; and notes that anger is not properly a synonym of resentment, being often justifiable when its cause is just and its expression restrained.
webster_full: ANGER, n. A violent passion of the mind excited by a real or supposed injury; usually accompanied with a propensity to take vengeance, or to obtain satisfaction from the offending party.

Anger is also excited by an injury offered to a relation, friend or party to which one is attached; and some degrees of it may be excited by cruelty, injustice or oppression offered to those with whom one has no immediate connection, or even to the community of which one is a member.
Nor is it unusual to see something of this passion roused by gross absurdities in others, especially in controversy or discussion.
Anger may be inflamed till it rises to rage and a temporary delirium.
scriptures: Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
Mar 3:5

And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.
John 2:15
And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;
Psa 7:11
God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day.
Jas 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
corruption_summary: A man's temper is baptised as righteous anger, and the tests Scripture supplies are all ones it fails.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 3:5 gives the signature and it is two emotions in one look: He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts. Grief is the article that is nearly always missing from the counterfeit. Righteous anger sorrows over the people it is aimed at and would be delighted to be made unnecessary by their repentance; the counterfeit enjoys itself, rehearses the offence, and is faintly disappointed when the offender turns out to have an explanation. That test is available to any man in about thirty seconds and is almost never applied.

The second test is the object. The Lord's recorded anger is provoked by hardness toward the suffering, by obstruction of the weak, by His Father's house made a market — never by an insult to Himself, and when He was reviled He reviled not again. Most anger that presents itself as righteous is aroused most reliably by offences against the angry man's own standing, and that single observation disposes of the majority of cases. Webster is unusually helpful here, allowing that anger may justly be roused by cruelty or oppression offered to strangers, and noting drily that it is also roused by gross absurdities in others, especially in controversy.

The third test is duration, and Ephesians 4:26 supplies it as a hard practical limit that bypasses self-assessment entirely: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Whatever the anger's merits, it has a curfew. Paul adds in the next verse the reason — neither give place to the devil — treating retained anger as an opening rather than a conviction. An indignation that survives the night is being kept, and a man keeping it should ask what for.
roots_summary: Greek orgizo (G3710), to be angry; orge (G3709), settled anger; parorgismos (G3950), provocation, wrath; sullupeomai (G4818), to be grieved with.
roots_lines: Greek orgizesthe kai me hamartanete (G3710) — be ye angry, and sin not; Ephesians 4:26, quoting Psalm 4:4.
Greek met' orges…sullupoumenos (G3709, G4818) — with anger, being grieved; Mark 3:5.
Greek orge anthropou (G3709) — the wrath of man; James 1:20.
usage: “With anger, being grieved” — and the grief is what is usually missing.
“Let not the sun go down upon your wrath” — a curfew, whatever the merits.
“The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” — however righteous it feels.

pos: n. phrase (the river of the water of life proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb; and the figure of the Spirit's supply in the believer)
etymology: The figure runs from Eden's four rivers through Ezekiel's temple stream to Revelation's crystal river, and the New Testament identifies its meaning: John says plainly that the living water spoken of is the Spirit.
biblical_def: The river of life is the last picture in the Bible: “And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Rev 22:1). Ezekiel saw it rising in the temple and deepening as it ran, and its property is stated: “every thing shall live whither the river cometh” (Eze 47:9). The psalm sets it against a city under siege: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psa 46:4). The Lord makes it internal and outbound: “He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). And to the woman at the well: it “shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines river as a large stream of water flowing in a channel on land towards the ocean, a lake or another river; and notes that the fresh waters of the earth are conveyed by rivers to the ocean.
webster_full: RIVER, n. A large stream of water flowing in a channel on land towards the ocean, a lake or another river.
It is larger than a rivulet or brook; but there are many small streams of water to which the name of river is given.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth.
2. The head or source of a river.
scriptures: Rev 22:1
And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.
Eze 47:9

And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh.
Psa 46:4
There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High.
John 7:38
He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
John 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
corruption_summary: The river is treated as a private supply, and every text that describes it has it running outward and reaching something dead.
corruption_paragraphs: John 7:38 has a direction that most devotional use of it reverses: out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. Not into him — through him and out. The next verse removes any doubt about what is meant: this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive. A believer is not a reservoir but a channel, and the supply is verified downstream. John 4:14 has the inward half — a well of water springing up into everlasting life — and the two together give the whole: a spring inside a man that does not stay inside him.

Ezekiel 47 is the most instructive of the passages because of what the prophet is made to do. He is measured out into the water four times — ankles, knees, loins, and then waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over — and the man with the line asks him, Son of man, hast thou seen this? The river deepens the further it gets from its source, which is the opposite of how rivers behave and the point of the vision. And where it arrives, the salt sea, it heals; every thing shall live whither the river cometh, and the fishers stand on the banks.

Psalm 46:4 is worth setting beside those, because it is written about a city with an army outside it. There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God — and Jerusalem had no river, only the Gihon spring feeding a tunnel under the wall. That is the figure exactly: a supply that does not run past the gate where the enemy can see it, quiet and hidden and entirely sufficient, in a psalm that begins God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Revelation 22 finally shows it in the open, proceeding from the throne, with the tree of life on either side and its leaves for the healing of the nations.
roots_summary: Greek potamos (G4215), a river; hudor zon (G5204), living water; pege (G4077), a spring, well; Hebrew nachal (H5158), a stream, torrent.
roots_lines: Greek potamos hudatos zoes (G4215, G5204) — river of water of life; Revelation 22:1, and rivers, John 7:38.
Greek pege hudatos hallomenou (G4077) — a well of water springing up; John 4:14.
Hebrew nachal (H5158) — stream, torrent, wadi; Ezekiel 47:5–9, Psalm 36:8.
usage: “Out of his belly shall flow” — through him, and out.
“Every thing shall live whither the river cometh” — and it ran to the salt sea.
“There is a river” — and Jerusalem had none that anyone could see.

pos: n. phrase (a title of God drawn from the margin of Isaiah 26:4; the everlasting Rock in whom His people trust)
etymology: The AV text of Isaiah 26:4 reads “everlasting strength”; the marginal reading is the rock of ages, rendering the Hebrew tsur olamim. Toplady's hymn of 1763 took its title from that margin, and the phrase has been sung ever since by people who never read the note.
biblical_def: The Rock of Ages is God as the unchanging refuge. Isaiah's charge is: “Trust ye in the LORD for ever: for in the LORD JEHOVAH is everlasting strength” (Isa 26:4) — where the margin reads, the rock of ages. The title is Moses' first: “He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he” (Deu 32:4). David piles it up: “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust” (Psa 18:2). Paul identifies it: the fathers “drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ” (1Co 10:4). And the Lord makes it the test of a life's foundation (Mat 7:24–25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rock as a large mass of stony matter, and, in Scripture, figuratively, defense, protection, refuge — and notes that God is called a rock, as the refuge and defense of his people.
webster_full: ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals, either bedded in the earth or resting on its surface.
2. In Scripture, figuratively, defense; means of safety; protection; strength; asylum.
The Lord is my rock. 2 Sam. 22.
3. Firmness; a firm or immoveable foundation.
4. A species of vulture or condor.
scriptures: Isa 26:4
Trust ye in the LORD for ever: for in the LORD JEHOVAH is everlasting strength:
Deu 32:4
He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
Mat 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
corruption_summary: The figure is heard as sentiment, and in Scripture a rock is chosen for one property: it does not move when everything else does.
corruption_paragraphs: The metaphor is not decorative and it is not about grandeur. In the terrain the psalms come out of, a rock is where a hunted man goes — a cleft, a crag, a height an enemy cannot easily reach — and David wrote most of these lines while being pursued through exactly that country. Webster catches it: in Scripture, figuratively, defense; means of safety; protection; asylum. When a psalm calls God a rock it is making a claim about survivability under attack, by a man who had tested the ordinary kind.

Deuteronomy 32:4 is the fullest statement and it defines the rock by moral rather than physical properties: his work is perfect, for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he. That is what makes Him a place to stand. A refuge that were merely powerful would be no refuge at all if it were arbitrary, and the whole comfort of the figure depends on the character clauses. Moses sings this in a song God told him to teach Israel against the day they would forget it.

First Corinthians 10:4 makes the identification explicit and the church has sung it ever since: that Rock was Christ. Paul is reading the wilderness narrative — the rock struck at Horeb, the water that followed a nation through forty years of desert — and saying the supply was a Person. Which is also why Toplady's hymn asks the Rock to be cleft for me, since the rock in Exodus gave water only after it was struck, and Numbers records what happened to the man who struck it a second time when he had been told to speak to it instead.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsur (H6697), a rock, cliff; olam (H5769), age, everlasting; sela (H5553), a crag, stronghold; Greek petra (G4073), a rock, bedrock.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsur olamim (H6697, H5769) — rock of ages; Isaiah 26:4 margin; tsur also Deuteronomy 32:4, 32:15, Psalm 18:2, 62:2.
Hebrew sela (H5553) — crag, cliff, stronghold; Psalm 18:2, 31:3, 40:2, Exodus 33:22.
Greek petra (G4073) — rock, bedrock; 1 Corinthians 10:4, Matthew 7:24–25, 16:18.
usage: “In the LORD JEHOVAH is everlasting strength” — margin: the rock of ages.
“He is the Rock, his work is perfect” — defined by character, not size.
“That Rock was Christ” — the supply was a Person.
